text:
We recently covered the “essay wars” in Lightbulb, in which Tony Blair, Keir Starmer and Andy Burnham fired off long missives on the state of the nation. It seems Nigel Farage was feeling left out, for yesterday he published the “first of many” articles on his new Substack account, titled “Britain is a two tier state—against white people”. (It has slightly more likes than my own Substack interview with Yanis Varoufakis, though a far more negative comments section. No one, as far as I know, called our discussion “horse sh*t.)The “white British” ethnic identity has been an increasing point of emphasis on Britain’s populist right—see Ben Ansell’s column from October 2025, in which he criticised Tory MP Neil O’Brien and other right-wingers for using the term. “Let’s call this turn what it is: racist,” he wrote. “This is racism of a type that mainstream politicians have not encouraged since the early 1980s.”As for Farage’s essay, he claims that the British police have become functionally “anti-white”—something he was adamant on in his public statements about Henry Nowak’s murder. But Alan Rusbridger begs to differ. “Before this lie passes into history and becomes the truth,” he writes, we ought to remember various recent investigations, from Hampshire to Charing Cross, that have found serious accusations of racism within police ranks. With this in mind, Alan questions whether anti-racism efforts within the police are really so unfounded.As we approach the ten-year anniversary of Brexit, Alan notes an irony here too: by allowing disinformation and racism to spread unchecked on social media, we are “​​taking back control from the unelected Brussels bureaucrats and handing it to Elon Musk, JD Vance, Nigel Farage, Tommy Robinson and a handful of faceless crypto billionaires.” Ah, the pure air of sovereignty!Speaking of connections between debates about race in the US and UK, CBS News has hired British broadcaster Trevor Phillips, who was previously suspended then readmitted to the Labour party over allegations of Islamophobia. Alan and Lionel Barber speak to NPR’s media correspondent David Folkenflik on Media Confidential about what’s going on at CBS, as controversial editor-in-chief Bari Weiss causes ructions, including at its flagship programme 60 Minutes.Alan has also been busy penning a profile of conductor Nil Venditti for our latest issue. A 31-year-old Italian-Turkish maestro, Venditti likes to talk with audiences before, after and even during performances—and her innovative approach has landed “like a small benign bomb exploding in the world of classical music.”Finally, Keir Starmer has announced a social media ban for under-16s, with Meta, YouTube and Snapchat all arguing that the policy will push teens into even less regulated spaces. It’s a great time to revisit Ethan Zuckerman’s essay from our last edition—a nuanced take on how to balance the harms and benefits of social media for kids. Email your thoughts on today’s news to ben.clark@prospectmagazine.co.uk.

Benjamin ClarkHead of digital audience
